title: Reading Practice 5 - The Development of Writing Systems
description: IELTS Academic Reading practice about the evolution of writing from pictographs to alphabets.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: The Development of Writing Systems
stimuli.content:
A The invention of writing is widely regarded as one of the most transformative developments in human history. Before writing, knowledge could only be transmitted orally, limiting the amount of information that could be preserved and shared across generations. The earliest known writing system, cuneiform, emerged in Mesopotamia around 3400 BCE. Initially consisting of simple pictographs pressed into clay tablets, cuneiform gradually evolved into a complex system of wedge-shaped marks that could represent not just objects but also abstract concepts and sounds.

B Around the same time, the ancient Egyptians developed their own writing system: hieroglyphics. Unlike cuneiform, Egyptian hieroglyphics maintained their pictorial quality throughout their history, though they also developed cursive forms called hieratic and demotic for everyday use. In China, the earliest known writing appeared on oracle bones during the Shang Dynasty around 1200 BCE. These inscriptions were used for divination, with questions being carved into turtle shells or animal bones that were then heated until they cracked.

C Perhaps the most revolutionary development in the history of writing was the invention of the alphabet. The first true alphabet, in which individual symbols represent individual consonant sounds, was developed by Semitic peoples in the Sinai Peninsula around 1800 BCE. This Proto-Sinaitic script was the ancestor of the Phoenician alphabet, which in turn gave rise to the Greek alphabet. The Greeks made a crucial innovation by adding symbols for vowels, creating the first complete alphabet.

D The impact of writing on human civilization cannot be overstated. Writing enabled the creation of legal codes, historical records, and literary works. It facilitated trade across vast distances and allowed governments to administer large territories. The development of printing technology, first in China and later in Europe with Gutenberg's press, amplified these effects enormously. Today, the digital age has created entirely new forms of writing, from email to social media.
